title: Efficiency as a ratio

learning_outcomes.text: recall and understand that the efficiency of a system is the ratio of useful energy output from the system to the total energy input

external_knowledge: A ratio compares two quantities of the same type.
A decimal ratio can be converted to a percentage by multiplying by 100%.
prerequisites.dependency_basis_note: The Topic 5 course map is absent from this checkout. The immediately previous package 9702_t05_cm03_l06 was read directly; its handoff permits kinetic-energy calculation, comparison and complete energy ledgers with dissipative transfers. The conservation retrieval is additionally grounded in controlled preceding outcome 9702_t05_m01_o02.

prior_knowledge_summary: Use E_K = 1/2 mv^2 and compare kinetic energies using the squared dependence on speed.
Use complete energy ledgers that include dissipative transfers.
Energy is transferred between stores and the total energy is conserved under controlled outcome 9702_t05_m01_o02.
new_learning: Efficiency compares useful output with total input using a dimensionless ratio.
Efficiency can be written as a decimal or a percentage.
The same ratio may use matching energy values or matching power values.
Energy conservation can check useful output, non-useful transfer and total input.
not_yet_taught: combining power with time through P = W/t or E = Pt
electrical circuit efficiency involving e.m.f. and internal resistance
rearranging the efficiency relationship to find an unknown input or output
multi-stage and overall-efficiency calculations reserved for 9702_t05_cm04_l08

blocks.heading: Where did the missing energy go?
content: A battery sends 100 J into a small fan, but only 62 J becomes useful kinetic energy of the moving air. Has 38 J disappeared?
Predict which two energies should be compared if we want one number that describes how well the fan meets its purpose.

figure.purpose: Create the need for efficiency while preserving energy conservation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show a 100 J input arrow entering a fan, a 62 J useful moving-air arrow leaving it and an unlabeled second output arrow. Do not reveal the missing energy value or an efficiency calculation.
figure.alt_text: A fan receives 100 joules and transfers 62 joules usefully, with another output transfer left for the learner to identify.

blocks.heading: Compare like with like
content: Efficiency asks what fraction of the total input reaches the useful output. The system purpose decides which output is useful.
Formula to remember: efficiency equals useful energy output divided by total energy input. The numerator and denominator must both be energies for the same operating interval.
For the fan, efficiency = 62/100 = 0.62 = 62%. The remaining 38 J is transferred in non-useful ways, so energy is conserved.

controlled_formula.name: Efficiency
controlled_formula.latex: \eta = \frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}} = \frac{\text{useful power output}}{\text{total power input}}

symbol_and_unit_notes: η is efficiency and has no unit because like quantities are divided.
Useful energy output and total energy input are measured in joules, J.
Useful power output and total power input are measured in watts, W.

figure.purpose: Anchor the numerator and denominator to a physical energy-flow picture.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Draw an energy-flow box with total input entering, useful output leaving on top and non-useful output leaving below. Place the exact controlled efficiency formula beside it. Use matching colours to link useful output to the numerator and total input to the denominator.
figure.alt_text: An energy-flow box links useful output to the numerator and total input to the denominator of the efficiency ratio.

blocks.heading: A fraction of every input packet
content: Imagine each 1.00 J of input energy as one packet. An efficiency of 0.72 means that, on average, 0.72 J from each packet reaches the useful output.
The same value may be written as 72%. The decimal 0.72 and the percentage 72% describe the same ratio, but 0.72% would be one hundred times too small.
A physical efficiency must lie from 0 to 1, or from 0% to 100%. A result above this range signals a reversed ratio, inconsistent quantities or an arithmetic error.

figure.purpose: Explain decimal and percentage forms with a part-whole representation.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show a strip of 100 small energy squares with 72 grouped as useful and 28 as other transfers. Label 0.72 equals 72 percent. Do not use a device context.
figure.alt_text: Seventy-two of one hundred energy squares represent an efficiency of 0.72 or 72 percent.

blocks.heading: Work from the purpose, then form the ratio
content: A food mixer receives 4.80 kJ of electrical energy. Its purpose is to move the mixture, and 3.36 kJ becomes useful kinetic energy.
First identify the useful output: 3.36 kJ. Then identify the total input: 4.80 kJ. Both values use the same unit, so no conversion is needed.
Independent check: 3.36 kJ + 1.44 kJ = 4.80 kJ, so the energy account balances.

figure.purpose: Model the complete identify, divide, convert and conserve procedure.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Use a four-step worked layout for the mixer: purpose, numerator and denominator, ratio calculation, then a separate energy-conservation check. Keep kJ on every energy line.
figure.alt_text: A worked mixer example calculates efficiency and checks that useful plus non-useful energy equals the input.

blocks.heading: The same ratio can use power
content: The controlled efficiency formula also permits useful power output divided by total power input when both powers describe the same steady operating condition.
A pump receives 250 W and delivers 185 W usefully to the water. Its efficiency is 185/250 = 0.740 = 74.0%.
Do not mix an energy in joules with a power in watts inside one ratio. Use energy over energy or power over power.

figure.purpose: Show why energy and power ratios are equivalent without introducing a new power formula.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show two aligned columns labelled energy during the same interval and power during steady operation. Connect useful over input in both columns. Include a crossed-out mixed J over W ratio.
figure.alt_text: Matching energy and power columns show valid efficiency ratios and reject mixing joules with watts.

blocks.heading: The largest number is not automatically the input
content: It can feel safe to put the larger value underneath because efficiency should be below one. That shortcut can hide a wrong system boundary.
Instead, read the stated purpose. Useful output belongs on top and total input belongs underneath. A heater may treat thermal energy as useful, while a motor may treat motion as useful.
If the ratio exceeds one, do not simply flip it. Recheck what entered the chosen system, what useful result left it and whether the values cover the same interval.

figure.purpose: Repair denominator guessing by making system purpose and boundary explicit.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Compare the same device under two stated purposes, with a boundary box and arrows. Highlight that the useful arrow changes with purpose. Include a small warning card: identify, do not guess by size.
figure.alt_text: Two purposes for one device show that useful output is chosen by purpose rather than by numerical size.

blocks.heading: A final ratio checklist
content: For a single system, first state its purpose. Then label the total input and the useful output before touching the numbers.
A desk fan receives 120 J and transfers 84 J usefully to moving air. Its efficiency is 84/120 = 0.70 = 70%.

A reliable method is: state the purpose, identify useful output and total input, choose matching energy values or matching power values, form useful over input, convert form if requested, then check that 0 ≤ η ≤ 1. Rearranging the ratio and combining several stages belong to the next lesson.

figure.purpose: Synthesize single-system ratio identification and protect the next-lesson boundary.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show one desk-fan system with 120 J input and 84 J useful moving-air output, followed by a ratio card 84/120 equals 0.70 equals 70 percent. Add a short identify-and-check flow. Put rearrangement and multi-stage work in a locked next-lesson box.
figure.alt_text: A desk fan example and checklist summarize a single-system efficiency ratio of 0.70.

evidence_basis.p1_status: outside the delegated Paper 2 evidence scope
evidence_basis.evidence_scope_note: All 16 complete P2 questions, official mark schemes and enrichment records containing the 17 formula-mapped efficiency leaves were reviewed. Later electrical, deformation, kinematics and gravitational-energy methods appearing in mixed questions are excluded from required lesson solutions.

concepts_taught: efficiency as useful output divided by total input
physical range from zero to one or zero to one hundred percent
misconceptions_addressed: A decimal efficiency and its percentage have the same numerical digits.
The larger number should always be the denominator.
Energy and power may be mixed in one ratio.
A result outside the physical range should be flipped without rechecking the system boundary.
next_lesson_can_assume: Identify useful output and total input from a stated system purpose.
Calculate a direct efficiency ratio in decimal or percentage form when useful output and total input are given.
Use energy conservation to check useful and non-useful transfers.
Check whether a decimal or percentage efficiency lies in its physical range.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Power defined as work done per unit time.
Use or derivation of P = W/t or P = Fv.
Electrical source efficiency involving internal resistance.
Reverse efficiency calculations or multi-stage overall efficiency.
